extracted.intended_audience: student journalists and journalism instructors (high school/college)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing informative interviews, news leads, datelines, and feature stories — focused on what makes effective journalism (especially for classroom/tyro reporters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of an interview lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the lead of each interview... What highlight is brought out? Who is interviewed? Identification? Occasion of the interview?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate interview leads by whether they present the highlight, identify who is interviewed, give the occasion, and foreground the most newsworthy element. (Exercises ask to quote passages of indirect discourse and note why they are used; also to note how the person is recalled and what verbs are used for 'said'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy in suggesting reporter's questions
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Queensberry interview, note the economy with which the reporter’s questions are suggested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the reporter implies questions succinctly rather than printing verbatim Q&A; economy helps flow and keeps emphasis on informative material. Consider reorganizing for clearer sequencing when economy is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying speaker as accepted authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Underline the substantive element that identifies the speaker as an accepted authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include identifiers (title, affiliation, role) that justify the speaker's statements; position of authority in sentence matters (see 'Fixing the authority' examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixing the authority (placement and attribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixing the authority ... Note position in the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a fact is justified by a sponsor, explicitly attribute it and decide where the authority phrase best sits in the sentence to make the claim credible (e.g., 'according to reports received by Newton Bright, Commissioner of Agriculture').

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributing uncorroborated claims (use of impersonal verbs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of constructions like 'It was learned', 'It was announced', 'It was rumored, it was reported' to justify facts presented by a sponsor when not corroborated by complete evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When information lacks complete corroboration, attribute to a source or use such impersonal constructions to avoid asserting unverified facts; this also guards against libel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be concrete with size/numbers (avoid vague crowd phrases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't say a large number, a big crowd. Size is relative. Be concrete. Quote figures or say more than or less than an estimated number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer exact figures or qualified estimates ('more than 300,000') instead of vague words; spell out numerals if they begin a sentence. Use concrete data to give readers scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number style in leads (spell out numerals at start)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out the figures if they form the first word of the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a numeral would start a lead, write it in words for readability and house style consistency (e.g., 'Forty thousand attended...' rather than '40,000 attended...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise word choice for persons/counts ('Persons not people')
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons not people — More than, not over 300,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to precise noun and preposition choices in formal news writing; prefer clear/legal/grammatical forms appropriate to the context and intended tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify persons to justify the story (source-fixing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the persons mentioned below to justify the story. For practice, make up the necessary facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A news item should show who is the sponsor/source of key claims; naming and qualifying that person strengthens the story's credibility and explains why the fact is reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never give an opinion in a news story
rubrics_metrics.description: Never give an opinion in a news story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report facts and attributed statements; opinions should be clearly labeled as such or left to editorial/feature contexts. Maintain objectivity in straight news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against libel when reporting uncorroborated statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Play up the news in each of the statements below on the authority of its sponsor. The news given has not been corroborated by complete evidence. You must guard against libel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing allegations or high-claim statements that are not fully verified, attribute them clearly, soften absolute assertions, and avoid repeating unverified damaging claims as fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use authority phrasing to present unverified claims safely
rubrics_metrics.description: The news given has not been corroborated by complete evidence. Play up the news ... on the authority of its sponsor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recast unverified but newsworthy items to stress the sponsor/source (e.g., 'is said to be', 'according to reports'), thereby preserving news value while reducing legal/ethical risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write correct datelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the date line for a story, dated January 12, 1928, and sent to your paper by an alumnus who is traveling in Brazil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard dateline formats (city, country/state, date) and show byline or sender context when appropriate; datelines locate the story and lend immediacy/authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature story purpose (human/dramatic elements and emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The feature story is a narrative which depends upon dramatic or human elements for interest... It is intended to create an emotional effect in the reader’s mind rather than to give straight news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame features to appeal to readers' emotions or curiosity; choose material that yields human drama, humor, pathos, or atmosphere rather than only conveying facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature openings: short-story beginning often best
rubrics_metrics.description: The feature story may or may not begin with the formal news lead—usually not. As a rule, the short story beginning is the most effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider narrative, scene-setting, or character openings rather than inverted-pyramid leads for features; the opening should establish tone and draw the reader into the single effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three hallmarks of a well-written feature: Unity, Dominant tone, Single effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Every well-written feature story is characterized by three things: Unity. Dominant tone. Single effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate features for whether every element supports one unified purpose, whether a consistent tone/atmosphere is sustained, and whether the piece aims at a single emotional or intellectual effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustain the opening note throughout (consistency of purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: The note struck in the opening paragraph must be sustained throughout. Whatever appeal it sets out to make it must accomplish without change of purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid shifts in purpose or tone mid-article; every paragraph and detail should reinforce the initial promise or mood established by the opening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature structure: not cuttable like a news article
rubrics_metrics.description: The feature story cannot be cut like the news article by removing paragraphs from the bottom upward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features are crafted as narratives or unified pieces; editors should consider integrity of flow and climax before trimming; cuts may require reworking rather than simple bottom pruning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of details and word choice create atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer creates the desired effect ... largely through the judicious selection of details and a choice of words that connote the 'color' of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose sensory, specific, and connotative details and tonal vocabulary that together build atmosphere; match diction to the intended dominant tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use color words in a color story
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Color Words in a Color Story
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a story's effect depends on vividness or scene-color, employ descriptive (color) words to enhance visual and emotional impact; avoid bland/general descriptors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature writer's aim: dramatist's aim ('Make 'em laugh; make 'em weep')
rubrics_metrics.description: The feature writer's aim is the dramatist’s aim: 'Make 'em laugh; make 'em weep.' The effect to be produced in the reader must govern the style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose narrative devices (climax, irony, surprise) and stylistic choices that serve the intended emotional reaction; style should be subservient to effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climax placement and possibility of surprise endings
rubrics_metrics.description: As in any dramatic narrative, the climax may come at the close. Indeed, a feature story may rival any O. Henry short story with its surprise ending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan pacing so that emotional or ironic payoff can occur at the most effective point (often the end); use surprise/climax deliberately to enhance single effect.
